The fact that some folks have the belief that Gentoo Linux is all about Maxxximum Performance doesn't change the fact that nearly all of the people who use it and -almost certainly- all of the people who maintain it strongly disagree with that claim.
> Regarding -O2 vs -O3, in the early days, -O3 was considered quite safe (I don't recall if it was recommended, but it wasn't discouraged). ... I went with -O3 because of guidance from the Gentoo folks.

It has been too long for me to remember what -O level my first Gentoo box ended up using (and I can't be bothered to pull it out of the closet and power it on to see), but the box I installed in ~2007 is using -O2. A random sampling of the few Gentoo forum posts from the early days that are in the Wayback Machine [0], as well as a handful of Bugzilla reports from the 2002->2005 era _suggests_ that most folks in the early days were using -O2. I'm certain that I played with all of the optimization levels on my first box, didn't notice any performance difference, and then settled on one that I can no longer remember.

And like, you say that -O3 wasn't discouraged. Well, -O3 isn't really discouraged today. The advice about -O3 gives you a summary of the facts and trusts you to make the choice that's right for you [1][2]

  WARNING: Using `-O3` may cause some packages to break either during the compilation or misbehave at runtime, although `-O3` retains standard conformance, hence any breakage is either undefined behaviour in the application, or (very rarely) a compiler bug.
  
  <irrelevant stuff elided>
  
  `-O3`: enables `-O2` as well as optimizations that are expensive in terms of compile time and memory usage. Compiling with `-O3` is likely to improve performance (although not guaranteed). While historically `-O3` could expose compiler bugs, nowadays issues with `-O3` are almost always instances of undefined behavior (UB) and the code is at fault and should be fixed. Some packages are still known-broken with `-O3`. Using `-O3` is not recommended unless running test suites for packages.
(I'm pretty sure that "unless running test suites" thing means "you shouldn't use this optimization level unless you're also using FEATURES="test" to run the package's tests".)

FWIW, it's my maybe-incorrect understanding that many (most? all?) packages that are known-broken with specific flags get those flags filtered out and replaced with known-good ones... unless they're nutball "ricer" flags, in which case the user gets told "Don't do that!".

Hi Hacker News! I'm Tim, and I made y'all some Pasta. :)

Others have New Year's resolutions to get fit, mine's to build an app in hopes of getting fit.

Fun fact, I built something like this over 10 years ago but never released it. Co-founder issues, if you must know. I called it Träna Fit, träna being the Swedish word for train. I remember hiring a voice actor on Fiverr to record every rep count.

Fast forward to today and the models are good enough to do much of this, and more. Pasta is a personal trainer app for iPhone. You ask for a workout by voice or text, Apple's Foundation Models build it, and a small voice model running on the phone (Kokoro-82M) guides you as you train.

When it comes to planning and generation, I have to admit it still has plenty of room for improvement. I grade what it writes with evals. My favorite catch so far: I asked for a 500 kg deadlift for 100 reps, and the model built it, no questions asked. I'm hoping to make the evals better as I get more feedback on what's working and what's not. Over time, I'd like it to come as close as possible to what a certified personal trainer would build for you based on your goals and needs.

I also realize that getting fit and working out isn't solely about knowing what to do. There's also the motivation + accountability part, and I do have some ideas on the roadmap that I'll share later. And I swear, it's not gamifying your health and fitness results.

You'll need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence on iOS 27, and it's free for 7 days. Give it a try. I'd love to know what you ask it for first, and whether you'd do the workout it builds.
